entry.title: Operators available in Regular Expressions (RegEx) in ABSL - hexadecimal values
entry.content:
Dear Experts,

We have a requirement to validate certain text fields by checking whether they contain any non-UTF-8 characters. For this purpose, we would like to use the built-in .FindRegex function for strings in ABSL. 

However, to achieve this, we need to reference the allowed characters by their hexadecimal values. Normally, this is done using escape tokens such as as \x or \u. For example, the following RegEx works correctly in standard implementations (see www.regex101.com😞

[^\x{0000}-\x{c5be}]

Unfortunately, this expression does not seem to be interpreted correctly by ABSL. It appears that ABSL can interpret escape tokens to some extent — for instance, the following RegEx works as expected:

[^\\x00-\\x99]

(The first backslash escapes the second one so that ABSL interprets it correctly.)

However, this pattern is limited to single-byte values only (from 00 fo FF) and we need to include all UTF-8 characters, which requires two-byte tokens such as the one in the earlier example.

I'm seeking general technical background information about the RegEx flavour used in C4C. Specifically, if it is based on PCRE2, because then it should support both \x63 and \x{0063} syntaxes. However, only the former seems to be recognized, which suggests either a different underlying standard is being used or there is an explicit limitation in functionality.

Could you please provide documentation or guidance on which operators are supported in ABSL for use in the .FindRegEx function?

Thank you and best regards,
Marek

entry.title: SAP Business ByDesign ABSL: Why Does the Same Logic Behave Differently in Different Scenarios?
entry.content:
If you have worked with ABSL in SAP Business ByDesign for a while, you may have come across a situation where your script works as expected in one scenario but not in another.

You check the code, review the conditions, and everything looks correct. Yet, when the same process is triggered in a different way, the expected result doesn't happen.

Before changing the code, it is worth checking how the script is being executed.

In ByDesign, the result doesn't always depend on the logic inside the script. The business object, the event being triggered, the data available at that point, and the way the record is created or updated can all affect the outcome.

Let's look at a few situations that are worth checking when troubleshooting ABSL.

1. Is the script actually being triggered?

One of the first things I would check is whether the script is being executed at all.

For example, you might have written validation logic in a BeforeSave script. It works when a user creates or updates a record through the UI, but the same validation doesn't appear to work when the record is created through another process.

It is tempting to assume that something is wrong with the condition or the script itself. However, the first question should be whether that operation invokes the expected logic.

When investigating this, check the following:

  • How is the business object record being created or updated?

  • Is the expected event supported and triggered for that operation?

  • Does the script execute but skip the logic because of a condition?

  • Is the record being processed through a different business object or operation?

These checks help narrow down the issue before you start changing the code.

2. Check the data available when the script runs

Sometimes, the script executes correctly, but the values available during execution are different from what you expect.

Consider a simple condition that checks a document status before executing some business logic.

if (this.StatusCode == "InTransfer")
{
    // Execute business logic
}

The code inside the condition will run only if the status matches the expected value.

If the record has a different status when the script executes, the condition won't be satisfied. This can happen when the logic depends on a value that is populated or updated at another stage of the process.

When debugging, compare the actual field values in the scenario that works with those in the scenario that fails.

Pay particular attention to status fields, identifiers, associations, and fields that may not be populated immediately.

Also, make sure the example field and status code above match the actual business object and code values used in your implementation.

3. Why does it work for one record but not for multiple records?

Another situation worth considering is when processing a single record works correctly, but processing multiple records produces unexpected results.

There are several possible reasons for this. One record may contain different input values, a condition may be satisfied for one record but not another, or an external request may return different results.

Instead of immediately modifying the script, compare the records individually.

For each record, check whether the expected script executes, whether the conditions are satisfied, and whether the required values are assigned and saved.

If the script calls an external API, also verify the request and response for each record. A successful response for one record doesn't necessarily mean that all subsequent requests will return the same data.

This is why testing with multiple records is important whenever the business process supports it.

4. The API call succeeds, but the fields are still empty

When working with integrations, another common area to investigate is the gap between retrieving data and seeing that data in the business object.

An external request can succeed without guaranteeing that the expected values are stored correctly.

For example, the issue could be related to the response structure, how the response is parsed, the field assignment, or the subsequent save operation.

I would check the flow in this order:

  1. Is the request being sent with the correct parameters?

  2. Does the response contain the expected values?

  3. Is the script reading the correct elements from the response?

  4. Are those values being assigned to the intended fields?

  5. Are the values persisted in the business object?

  6. If the values are persisted, are the relevant UI fields correctly configured to display them?

Checking each stage separately makes it easier to identify where the problem actually occurs.

If the data is already saved but is not visible on the screen, there may be no need to change the integration logic at all.

5. A few things I check before changing ABSL code

When an ABSL script doesn't behave as expected, I find it useful to start with a few basic questions:

  • Is the correct business object and event involved?

  • Does the script execute in the scenario where the issue occurs?

  • Are the field values and conditions what I expect them to be at runtime?

  • Is any part of the logic dependent on another service or process?

  • Does the issue occur with every record or only specific records?

  • Are the values missing from the saved data, or are they simply not visible in the UI?

These questions may sound simple, but they help separate an execution issue from a logic issue or a data issue.

It is also worth reproducing the problem in a test environment before making changes to a working implementation.

Final thoughts

ABSL troubleshooting is not always about finding an error in the code. Sometimes, the more important part is understanding when the script runs, what data is available at that point, and how the business process reaches that stage.

When something works in one scenario but fails in another, I would start by comparing the execution paths rather than rewriting the logic straight away.

Understanding that difference can save a lot of debugging time, especially when working with custom business objects and integrations in SAP Business ByDesign.

Have you encountered similar behaviour with ABSL? It would be interesting to hear how other developers approach these situations, particularly when the same business logic is triggered through different processes.
